title: Darwin spent months hunting a rare rhea, then ate one by mistake

cover.alt: Charles Darwin grins beside a roast bird on a platter on the Patagonian plain at dusk, holding a fork; in the distance a live rhea looks on in alarm.

body: On the voyage of HMS Beagle, **Charles Darwin** kept hearing from gauchos about a second, smaller kind of rhea, the 'Avestruz Petise': darker and mottled, with shorter legs. At Port Desire in Patagonia the ship's artist, Conrad Martens, shot a rhea, and Darwin, taking it for a young common rhea, helped eat it. 'It was cooked and eaten before my memory returned,' he wrote. The head, neck, legs, wings, many feathers and much of the skin had been kept, and from them a nearly perfect specimen was put together in London. In 1837 John Gould named it *Rhea darwinii*. Today it is *Rhea pennata*, the lesser rhea, because Alcide d'Orbigny had already named it. As a student at Cambridge, Darwin had belonged to a dining club that tried hawk and bittern and gave up at an old brown owl.

slides.alt: Charles Darwin, young and side-whiskered, in a wide hat, gallops across the plain on a brown horse, whirling a set of bolas, three balls on cords, round his head.
slides.caption: Uruguay, on the voyage of HMS Beagle. The young naturalist Charles Darwin decides to master the gauchos' bolas.

bubbles.text: How hard can it be? You just whirl them round your head.
bubbles.speaker: Charles Darwin

slides.alt: Darwin sits stunned on his horse, whose hind legs are tangled in the bolas cords. Two gauchos in wide black hats double up with laughter.
slides.caption: A ball hits a bush, and the bolas wrap round his own horse's hind leg. Luckily the horse is an old hand and stands still.

bubbles.text: We've seen every sort of animal caught, but never a man caught by himself!
bubbles.speaker: A gaucho

slides.alt: On the dry Patagonian plain, Darwin, holding his notebook, listens wide-eyed to a gaucho in a white shirt and red neckerchief. Far off, two rheas walk by.
slides.caption: Rio Negro, Patagonia. The gauchos tell him about a rare small rhea, the Avestruz Petise.

bubbles.text: Smaller than the common one, dark and mottled, with shorter legs. Easier to catch with bolas, too.
bubbles.speaker: A gaucho

slides.alt: Conrad Martens, in a cap and blue jacket, aims a long gun across the plain by an estuary. Smoke puffs from the muzzle; a rhea in the distance jumps.
slides.caption: Port Desire, Patagonia. The Beagle's artist, Conrad Martens, shoots a rhea for the pot.

slides.alt: Dusk on the plain. Darwin and a naval officer stand by a camp fire, each happily chewing a roast drumstick.
slides.caption: Darwin takes it for a young common rhea. It is roasted, and it is very good.

slides.alt: Darwin, drumstick in hand, freezes in horror over the carcass of the roast bird on its platter.
slides.caption: Then his memory returns. In his own words: 'It was cooked and eaten before my memory returned.'

bubbles.text: Wait. Short legs. Dark. Mottled. Oh no.
bubbles.speaker: Charles Darwin

slides.alt: Darwin grins at a wooden crate. Sticking out of it are a rhea's long neck and head, two scaly legs and a few grey feathers.
slides.caption: The head, neck, legs, wings, many feathers and much of the skin are saved. The rest has been digested.

bubbles.text: Pack it carefully. It's a new species, mostly.
bubbles.speaker: Charles Darwin

slides.alt: A panelled room in London. The ornithologist John Gould gestures proudly at a mounted rhea on a plinth while Darwin, now in a dark suit, smiles modestly.
slides.caption: London, 1837. From what was left, John Gould describes a new species and names it after him: Rhea darwinii.

bubbles.text: Named in your honour, Mr Darwin. Delicious, I'm told.
bubbles.speaker: John Gould

slides.question: Why was Darwin's specimen of the new rhea incomplete?
options: A puma ate half of it
It was cooked and eaten first
slides.explanation: Martens shot it at Port Desire, and Darwin, forgetting all about the Petise, took it for a young common rhea. The head, neck, legs, wings, feathers and much of the skin survived dinner.

source.label: Charles Darwin, The Voyage of the Beagle (1845), chapter V
